title: 608 Students Flee Maharashtra Ashram School as Ghost Rumours Trigger Mass Hysteria
excerpt: Doctors attribute the episodes of laughing, crying, and apparent possession to mass psychogenic illness, a well-documented phenomenon in residential schools.
body:
• More than 600 students fled an ashram school hostel in Maharashtra after reports of ghost sightings and claims that some girls were "possessed," according to NDTV, the Times of India, and other outlets.
  • Students reported hearing sounds of anklets and laughter at night, with some girls exhibiting episodes of uncontrollable laughing, crying, and then going numb.
  • Medical teams who examined the students found no physical illness; doctors attributed the episodes to mass psychogenic illness, commonly known as mass hysteria.
  • The incident mirrors similar episodes at Indian boarding schools in recent years, which psychologists link to stress, separation anxiety, and the high-pressure environment of residential institutions.

More than 600 students have fled an ashram school hostel in Maharashtra after a wave of ghost rumours and claims of supernatural possession swept through the residential facility, triggering what doctors are calling a case of mass psychogenic illness.

What Happened

The episode unfolded over several days at the Maharashtra ashram school, where 608 students — predominantly girls — abandoned the hostel after a series of disturbing incidents, according to reports from NDTV, the Times of India, WION, and India Today.

https://x.com/WIONews/status/2089239524933329271

Students described hearing unexplained sounds of anklets and laughter at night. Several girls reportedly began exhibiting alarming symptoms: uncontrollable laughing followed by crying, then going numb and unresponsive. Some students claimed their peers had become "possessed," and rumours of ghostly apparitions spread rapidly through the dormitory.

The cascade of fear accelerated quickly. As word spread from room to room, students who had not witnessed any incidents themselves began experiencing similar symptoms. Within days, parents began arriving to pull their children out. By the time authorities intervened, 608 of the hostel's residents had left.

Doctors Point to Mass Anxiety

Medical professionals who examined the affected students found no evidence of physical illness, poisoning, infection, or chemical exposure. Doctors attributed the episodes to mass anxiety — a well-documented psychological phenomenon in which emotional distress spreads rapidly through tightly bonded groups, manifesting as physical symptoms.

The condition, formally known as mass psychogenic illness, occurs when anxiety in a closed community escalates to the point where individuals develop genuine physical responses — fainting, trembling, crying, or temporary loss of motor control — despite the absence of any organic cause. The phenomenon is especially prevalent in boarding schools and residential institutions where young people live in close quarters under structured, high-pressure conditions.

"In tightly bonded groups, emotional distress can spread rapidly, taking physical form. When a child collapses and screams, it does not feel psychological. It feels real. It feels dangerous."

— Analysis of similar school incident, December 2025

A Pattern Across Indian Schools

The Maharashtra incident is far from isolated. Similar episodes have occurred at Indian boarding schools and hostels in recent years, following a strikingly consistent pattern: an initial report of a strange sighting or unexplained event, followed by rapidly spreading fear, then physical symptoms appearing in students who were not originally involved.

In 2025, students at a school in Mohancherra were hospitalized after a boy reported seeing a "headless human figure" in a bathroom. The panic quickly spread to his classmates. That same year, a Jharkhand school was closed temporarily after multiple girls exhibited symptoms of "possession" — episodes that psychologists later attributed to mass psychogenic illness. In an earlier incident, all 50 residents of the Kasturba Gandhi Girls' Hostel vacated after repeated sightings of a figure dressed in white.

British psychiatrist Simon Wessely, who has studied mass hysteria for three decades, has documented hundreds of similar episodes in single-sex boarding schools across Asia. He has described a familiar pattern: adolescent girls separated from their families, living in "a very regimented environment," with limited channels to express dissatisfaction. The symptoms — fainting, collapsing, neurological irregularities, and culturally influenced behaviors like possession — tend to begin with one person and spread through social networks within the institution.

Between Science and Belief

Despite clear medical explanations, episodes of mass psychogenic illness remain deeply unsettling for the communities involved. Parents and families often find it difficult to accept that their children's dramatic physical symptoms — the screaming, the collapse, the apparent unconsciousness — can originate from psychological rather than supernatural causes.

The language used to describe these events often shifts quickly from medical to spiritual. In past incidents, priests have been invited to perform rituals, and ashram administrators have faced pressure from parents demanding explanations beyond what psychiatry can offer.

What Comes Next

Authorities are working to reassure parents and students so that normal schooling can resume at the Maharashtra facility. In past cases, schools have typically reopened within days to weeks after medical assessments and counseling sessions, though the reputational damage to residential institutions can linger far longer.

Mental health experts say the incidents highlight a broader need for psychological support systems in India's network of roughly 100,000 residential schools and ashram institutions. Access to trained counselors, better communication channels between students and families, and reduced stigma around mental health could help prevent future episodes — or at least ensure they are recognized and addressed before panic takes hold.
nri_angle: The incident highlights mental health gaps in India's residential school system, a concern for diaspora families who support or consider ashram-style education for children in India.
